sections.name: What the research says, and what it does not.

items.text: The first offer · What it means
What the research says, and what it does not.
What the evidence says

The best measurement of first bids against final prices comes from public companies, because their filings record every bid. In 841 acquisitions of S&P 1500 companies between 2005 and 2019, the winning bidder’s first bid carried an average premium of 28.6 percent and the final price 38.2 percent. Only 8 percent of winners won with a single bid. Where the seller countered, which 44 percent did, the final price landed between the last bid and the counter two times in three. The first number was the opening of a negotiation, not the result of one.

Who starts the deal matters as much as how it is run. Target-initiated deals carry lower premiums, lower announcement returns and lower multiples of earnings than deals a buyer initiated, and the gap widens the less the buyer can confirm. A seller who approaches a single buyer is telling that buyer two things: that there is no competing bid yet, and that the seller has a reason to sell. The buyer prices both.
What the evidence does not say

It does not say that an auction beats a negotiation, or that more bidders means a higher price. The most cited study of how firms are sold found that target shareholders did about as well in negotiations with one buyer as in auctions with several, and the 2023 study above found final premiums similar regardless of the number of bids. What raises the price is not the count of bidders. It is that the buyer who knows a competing bid is possible prices against it from the first round, and that a seller who knows what the market would pay does not accept a number below it. Both depend on someone seeing the whole market.
The buyer who approaches you alone is not paying a premium for the privilege. In their own words, the attraction of an off-market deal is that there is less competition and the price is attractive.
Private equity firms, quoted in Unquote, October 2015
What an adviser changes for a private seller

The one study built on private sellers found that, after correcting for which sellers choose to hire an adviser, represented sellers received higher valuations, and that the acquirer’s own shareholders did slightly worse when the seller was represented, which is the same finding read from the other side. The size of the effect is disputed by the firms that cite the study, so we do not quote it here. The direction is not disputed.

What an adviser actually does is narrower than the word suggests. The adviser knows which buyers are active in the sector and at what price, so the first offer is read against a market rather than against hope. The adviser assembles the evidence before the buyer asks for it, so the price survives diligence. And the adviser carries the negotiation, so the owner can keep running the business the buyer is paying for. The valuation gap that kills half of all engagements is a gap between what the owner expects and what the records support; the work is on the records.
The terms behind the headline

A price is a headline. The terms decide what the seller receives. In the lower middle market in the second quarter of 2026, sellers received between 83 and 92 percent of the price in cash at closing, with the rest in seller financing, earnouts and retained equity. Earnouts appeared in 24 percent of private-target deals in 2025, and in 35 percent of deals under $25 million. Across the deals that had one, about 21 cents of every dollar of maximum earnout was paid. Rollover equity averaged 16.9 percent of enterprise value in private equity deals through the third quarter of 2025. An escrow without representation and warranty insurance ran a median 10 percent of the price.
A first offer with an earnout, a seller note and a rollover can carry a headline well above a second offer paid in cash, and deliver less. Reading the terms is the second half of reading the offer.
The time it takes

Lower-middle-market engagements took eleven to twelve months from signing with an adviser to closing in the second quarter of 2026, and 60 to 90 percent of sellers across five size segments arrived with less than a year of exit planning. In a 2018 survey of owners, three quarters believed they could sell within a year. The gap between those two figures is the time an unsolicited offer takes advantage of.
